You are checking a fictional interview transcript against the fact sheet it was written from. The transcript is part of a fair-play logic puzzle, so a single wrong or extra detail can ruin it.

FACT SHEET
R0: My kitchen clock is a quarter of an hour fast. I keep it so on purpose, so nothing is ever late.
R1: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at thirteen minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven.
R2: We heard Madame's piano begin at two minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and stop at eleven minutes past eleven by my kitchen clock.
R3: I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed thirteen minutes past eleven.

For each fact: "exact" if the transcript states all of it with the same timepiece and the same reading or relation (wording may differ); "altered" if any timepiece, reading, order, person or place differs, or part is missing; "missing" if absent. Then list only the sentences that give a detective NEW information about the evening between dinner and the temple striking eleven, information the fact sheet does not already give: a new clock or watch reading or time of day; a length of time or an order between two events of the evening; a person being somewhere, or moving, at a moment the sheet does not cover; a new sound heard at a particular moment; a claim that some clock is fast or slow. Do NOT list anything that merely restates or colours a fact on the sheet, feelings, opinions, descriptions of people or rooms, habits ("he does it every year"), the past before that night, the quarrel at dinner, which music was played, or the finding of the body. When in doubt whether something is new, ask: could a detective work out a time, an order or a whereabouts from it that the sheet alone does not give? If not, leave it out. Then rate the writing 1-10 as period prose a reader would enjoy.

TRANSCRIPT
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, cook and maid, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Good morning, Mademoiselle Häfeli. Thank you for waiting. Please sit down. You are not in trouble. I only want you to tell me, in your own way, how the evening went in the kitchen.

ROSA: Ja, I am sitting. Herrgott, I have been sitting since your men came up the stairs. I do not know what to do with my hands.

MATTHEY: Then rest them on the table. Tell me about the kitchen first.

ROSA: It is my kitchen. Everything was ready for the toast. I had washed the champagne glasses myself that afternoon and polished them twice, because Monsieur looks at glasses before he looks at the food. For the new century the glasses were on the tray and the bread was cut.

MATTHEY: You keep a clock in the kitchen.

ROSA: My kitchen clock, the American one on the shelf by the stove, is a quarter of an hour fast. I keep it so on purpose, so nothing is ever late. The soup is never late, Madame's coffee is never late. Monsieur used to laugh at me for it.

MATTHEY: You are sure of the quarter hour?

ROSA: I am sure. I set it myself, every Sunday, for ten years.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the evening, when you were in the kitchen.

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at thirteen minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven. She was white. She sat on the stool and did not say much. I gave her a cup of coffee and she did not drink it. She is a good girl, she does not complain.

MATTHEY: Go on, please.

ROSA: We heard Madame's piano begin at two minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock. Chopin. Fräulein Lina and I sat and listened, and it was beautiful, Herrgott, it was beautiful, and the kitchen was warm. Then it stopped at eleven minutes past eleven by my kitchen clock. I looked at the clock then because I wanted to get on with the glasses.

MATTHEY: Did you hear the hall clock?

ROSA: The old Morbier in the hall, yes. I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed thirteen minutes past eleven. I did not think about it. I was thinking about the bread.

MATTHEY: And after that?

ROSA: After that I went up to fetch the master for the toast. I went up the back stairs to the atelier, and I called to him, and he did not answer. He was on the floor under the long windows. I will not tell you more than that, Monsieur, I cannot. The regulator on the wall had stopped, and his hand was closed on his watch. I thought, he is only fallen asleep, and he will be cross that I woke him. Then I saw his face.

MATTHEY: You went for help?

ROSA: I went down. I did not run, I walked, because I did not want to frighten anyone. I found Madame, and she knew before I said a word. Then I did not know which to do first, so I did both.

MATTHEY: You are loyal to Madame.

ROSA: Loyal? I have been in this house twenty-two years. I would not leave her now.

MATTHEY: Do you fear the police, Mademoiselle?

ROSA: Ja. I am from the Emmental, we do not like men in uniform in our kitchens. I have done nothing wrong. But I am only a cook, and I do not know what a cook is supposed to say to a sûreté inspector at this hour. So I say what I saw, and I say it slowly, and if I am wrong about a minute you must forgive me.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Mademoiselle. That is very clear.

ROSA: Then may I go back to my kitchen? The bread will not wait.
